title: Sorrows of the Moon
text:
Tonight the moon dreams more lazily,

As if she were a beauty sunk among cushions

Who with discreet and very light hand caresses,

Before falling asleep, the contour of her breast.


On the silk back of sliding clouds,

Dying, she gives herself to prolonged ecstasies,

And lets her gaze wander over white visions

That rise into the blue like flowerings.


When upon this globe, with idle languor,

She lets a furtive tear roll down,

A pious poet, enemy of sleep,


Catches the cold drop in the hollow of his hand

like a fragment of opal with iridescent reflections.

And keeps it in his breast, far from the voracious sun.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the moon's languid body, opal tear, and the sleepless poet preserving it from the sun.

title: The Venal Muse
text:
You who love palaces, oh muse of my life,

Will you have, when Boreas is lord of January,

While snow falls through tedious evenings,

A brand to warm your violet feet?


Will you perhaps revive your marble shoulders

In the nocturnal rays filtering through the shutters?

Will you aid your purse and your bloodless throat

With the gold that gleams in the blue vault?


You must, to earn your nightly bread,

Swing the censer like a choirboy

And chant

Te Deums

in which you scarcely believe,

Repeating your charms, like a hungry clown,

And your laughter veiled by secret tears,

To see the vulgar guffaw burst out.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the muse's poverty and forced performance, from incense to clowning laughter.

title: To a Passerby
text:
The deafening street howled around me.

Tall, slender, in mourning, with a queenly sorrow,

A lady passed, who with sumptuous gesture

Gathered, swaying, the folds of her veils,


Most agile and noble, with two marble legs.

Suddenly I drank, with a madman's spasm,

And in her livid gaze, center of a thousand tempests,

The pleasure that annihilates, the paralyzing honey.


A lightning flash. Night. Fugitive beauty

Whose gaze made me, in one blow, be born again.

Except in eternity, shall I never see you again?


In any case far away, too late, perhaps never!

For I do not know where you fled, nor do you suspect my route,

You whom I would have loved. Oh you, who knew it!
editorial_note: The translation preserves the famous instant of urban encounter: lightning, loss, and impossible recognition.

title: What Will You Say Tonight, Poor Solitary Soul...
text:
What will you say tonight, poor solitary soul,

What will you say, heart, so recently withered,

To the very beautiful, the very good, the most beloved,

Beneath whose gaze you flowered again?


—We will employ pride in singing her praises;

Nothing equals the charm there is in her authority;

Her spiritual flesh has an angelic perfume,

And her eyes clothe us in the purest garments.


In the middle of night and solitude,

Or through the streets, surrounded by the crowd,

Her phantom dances in the air like a torch.


Sometimes she speaks and says: "I am beautiful and command

That for love of me you love only Beauty;

I am the Guardian Angel, the Muse, and the Madonna."
editorial_note: The translation keeps the soul's address to its beloved apparition as angel, muse, and Madonna.

title: The Death of Artists
text:
How long must I shake my bells

And kiss your forehead, sad caricature?

To hit the target, of mystical virtue,

How many arrows must my quiver waste?


In the subtlest feints we will spend our soul,

And more than one frame we must destroy,

Before contemplating the finished Creature

Whose infernal desire fills us with sobs.


There are some who never knew their idol,

Accursed sculptors marked by opprobrium,

Who beat with fury upon breast and brow,


With no more than one hope, dark Capitol!

That Death, hovering like a renewed sun,

Will finally make the flowers of their mind burst open.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the artist's exhausting search for the finished creature and death as the final flowering.
